summary_html: CPS **screens out** a report (no investigation) or closes as **unfounded** after minimal review. Federal law (CAPTA) conditions funding on operating screening criteria and recordkeeping; federal reviews (CFSR) assess decision quality.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — screening & intake system requirements  
- **CFSR Regulations (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal performance/quality review of state screening and responses

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit reversed, holding that a state agency's continued retention of child abuse investigation records after a report is ruled out or unsubstantiated violates neither substantive nor procedural due process, because retention serves legitimate child welfare interests and confidentiality provisions prevent any cognizable stigma.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling Fourth Circuit authority that a screened-out or unsubstantiated file may lawfully be retained by the agency.
key_cases.quote: The record before us presents no substantive due process violation of a familial privacy liberty interest by virtue of the retention of the Hodge investigation report.

key_cases.case_name: Norfolk Department of Human Services v. Goldberg
key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed an order releasing CPS investigation records, holding that the bad faith disclosure exception in Code § 63.2-1514(D) reaches reports conveyed to the Department by an innocent mandatory reporter when the underlying allegation originated with someone acting maliciously or in bad faith.
key_cases.relevance: It governs the records consequences of an unfounded disposition and the subject's route to obtain the investigative file.
key_cases.quote: Consistent with the statute’s purpose, we find that Code § 63.2-1514(D) covers bad faith disclosures made to mandatory reporters.

key_cases.case_name: Commissioner, Virginia Department of Social Services v. Fulton
key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia reversed a circuit court that had converted a founded disposition to unfounded and purged the registry, holding that under the Administrative Process Act the reviewing court may reject agency factfinding only if a reasonable mind would necessarily reach a different conclusion, and may not reweigh witness credibility.
key_cases.relevance: It shows what a circuit court may and may not do when asked to convert a founded disposition to unfounded and purge the record.
key_cases.quote: It is not the trial court’s role to determine the credibility of the witnesses.

timeline_requirements.deadline: No clock set by rule - initial safety assessment of the child's circumstances and threat of danger or harm, and a safety plan where appropriate, in both family assessments and investigations; the first face-to-face contact with the child is due within the response time set at intake, or within 24 hours when the victim child is younger than two (22VAC40-705-80(A)(1), (B)(1))
timeline_requirements.starts_from: The worker's first contact in the family assessment or investigation

timeline_requirements.deadline: 45 days (extendable to a total of 60 days on written justification, or to 90 days in a joint law-enforcement investigation)
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Statute sets no penalty; any extension requires written justification and the local department must notify the alleged abuser or neglector and the child's parents (Va. Code § 63.2-1505(B)(5); 22VAC40-705-120)
